transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well, thank you for having me. I, uh, I appreciate you taking the time. I suppose I'm here because... well, things at work have just gotten incredibly difficult lately, and it's starting to really bother me. I'm a library assistant—been doing clerical work and helping out in the back for years, you know, nothing too complicated, mostly just keeping things organized. But recently, my mind just feels completely... foggy. Like it's wrapped in thick wool or something, and I just can't seem to shake it. 

I'll sit down at my desk with my old cataloguing notes—notes I wrote myself, mind you, things I should know like the back of my hand—and I just stare at them. I cannot even keep my place on the page. I'll read the same line three or four times and it just doesn't register. And then, well, because I can't process what I'm looking at, I end up just sitting there, completely unable to decide what simple thing to do next. I mean, we're talking about basic, everyday tasks, like whether I should sort the return cart or update the system log, and I just... I can't choose. The fog is just so thick, I can't seem to string two thoughts together to make a simple decision about my day. It's just very frustrating at my age to suddenly feel like I can't do the job I've done forever.
When you think back, did this foggy, hard-to-concentrate feeling come on gradually over a long time, or did you notice it start more suddenly within the last few weeks or months?

Well, let me think about that. It’s a good question, because you’d think a person would remember the exact minute something like this starts, but... well, it certainly hasn't been happening for years, if that's what you mean. But it wasn't just yesterday, either. I'd say it’s been going on for about three months now. Yes, roughly three months. And I can pinpoint that fairly well because it started right around the time I began preparing to leave the library. 

You see, after being there so long, getting ready to leave is... well, it's quite a process. There are files to hand over, procedures to document for whoever takes my desk next, and I really wanted to leave everything in perfect order. But right when I started getting all that transition paperwork together, that’s when this heavy, low mood really settled in on me. And the fogginess, too. 

For these past three months, it has been there most days. Almost every single day, really. I’ll wake up, pour my morning coffee, and just hope my head feels clear for once, but... no. It’s just this constant, low feeling, day in and day out. And it makes trying to pack up my desk and organize my departure just impossibly frustrating, because I want to do a good job tying up loose ends, but most days I just sit there staring at the boxes, feeling completely bogged down by it all.
Besides the low mood and fogginess, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy over these past three months?

Well, you know, it's funny you should ask that, because I was just thinking about it the other day when I was looking at my watercolor books. I've always loved watercolors. For years, I'd come home from the library, make myself a cup of chamomile tea—sometimes Earl Grey if it was a chilly afternoon, but usually chamomile—and I'd sit by the window in the kitchen where the light is just right. I'd spend hours just painting landscapes, mostly trees and little streams, nothing professional, just for my own enjoyment, you know? It was always such a peaceful way to unwind after dealing with the Dewey Decimal System all day. 

But lately... lately, it's like you said. Most days, I just sit there at the kitchen table, and it's as if all the color has just drained out of everything. The whole world just feels gray and muted. I'll look at my paints, my favorite brushes—the ones I bought at that little art supply store downtown before it closed a few years back—and I just feel this immense, crushing heaviness. I don't feel any spark, any desire to pick up a brush. Even looking at the watercolor books, the ones with the beautiful instructional pictures that used to inspire me so much, they just make me feel so... tired. Heavy. I used to get lost in mixing the perfect shade of green for a pine tree, but now, the thought of even opening the paint box just feels like lifting a boulder. It's not just the painting, either. It's almost everything. It's like the joy has just evaporated, leaving behind this thick, gray sludge that I'm constantly trying to wade through. I just sit there staring out the window, feeling completely empty, wondering where all my enthusiasm went. It's a terrible feeling, really, to look at something you've loved for decades and just feel absolutely nothing but a heavy weight in your chest.

Over these past few months, have you also found yourself worrying excessively about various things—like your health, finances, or the future—more than you can control, even when there's no clear reason to worry?

Well, worrying... no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, my brother Tom, now he is a worrier. He’ll call me up on a Tuesday night fretting about the stock market or his blood pressure or whether the roof is going to hold up through the winter, but for me, it’s not really like that at all. 

Take my finances, for example. I’ve been at the county library system for over thirty years now, and they have a very solid municipal pension plan. I actually sat down with the HR director—Susan, lovely woman, always keeps a little crystal bowl of peppermint candies on her desk—about two years ago to map it all out. We went through all the paperwork, so I know I’m perfectly fine on that front. The house is paid off, my expenses are low. And my health... well, aside from this terrible gray fog and the heaviness we’ve been talking about, my physical health is quite alright. My regular doctor checked my cholesterol just last fall and told me I had the numbers of a man ten years younger. 

So, you see, there isn't really anything clear to worry about, and I don't find myself sitting around wringing my hands over the future out of nowhere. It’s actually quite the opposite of worry, if that makes any sense to you? Worry feels like... well, like your engine is revving too fast, like you’re pacing the floors and chewing your fingernails. I’m certainly not pacing. I can barely get myself out of the kitchen chair to even look at my watercolors, let alone pace. It’s more of a sinking feeling than a worrying one. I just sit there in the quiet, not really fretting over bills or what’s going to happen next year, just feeling completely stuck in the mud. So, no, no excessive worrying. Just... just that heavy, empty feeling.
How has your sleep been over these past three months—are you having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or sleeping more than usual?

Well, sleep... sleep has become quite a trial lately, to be completely honest with you. It’s a strange thing, because you’d think with how heavy and exhausted I feel all day, I’d just sleep straight through till morning. And I do go to bed incredibly tired. By the time ten-thirty rolls around, after I've watched the local news—I never watch the national news right before bed, it's just too much noise—I am practically dragging myself down the hall to the bedroom. My bones just ache with that tiredness. 

So falling asleep isn't the issue at all. I usually drift off the minute my head hits the pillow. But staying asleep... well, that’s an entirely different story. 

Almost like clockwork, every single night, my eyes will just pop open. The room will be pitch black, and the house is so quiet you can hear the refrigerator humming all the way from the kitchen. I’ll roll over and look at the digital clock on my nightstand—it’s one of those older models with the bright red numbers, I think I bought it at a Sears back in the late nineties—and it almost always says four in the morning. Sometimes it's three-fifty-five, sometimes it's four-ten, but it is always right around four. 

And once I'm awake at that hour, that is simply the end of my sleep for the night. I don't toss and turn, really, I just lie there flat on my back, staring up at the ceiling in the dark. And my mind just gets stuck. I just lie there thinking about what I am supposed to do with myself now. You know, with leaving the library after thirty years, and having all this empty time stretching out ahead of me... I just stare into the dark, feeling that terrible heavy emptiness we talked about, and I wonder how I'm going to fill the hours if I can't even bring myself to pick up a paintbrush anymore. I don't feel panicked, exactly, it's not a racing feeling, but I just lie there for hours, wide awake, turning that same thought over and over until the sun finally comes up. It makes the days feel incredibly long, let me tell you.
During this time, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, feeling like life isn't worth living, or that you'd be better off not being here?

Oh, heavens, no. No, no, nothing like that at all. I know I’ve been sitting here going on and on about this terrible gray fog, and how I just lie awake at four in the morning staring up at the ceiling, but... well, wanting to not be here? Hurting myself? No, absolutely not. 

It’s a very distinct difference, I think. I might feel like a useless old piece of furniture sitting in the kitchen, especially with my time at the library coming to a close. You know, when you’ve spent thirty years making sure the periodicals are perfectly organized—because let me tell you, some of the younger assistants, they just shove the magazines back on the shelves willy-nilly without checking the dates or the issue numbers—you get so used to having a clear, defined purpose. So losing that purpose makes me feel incredibly heavy and, well, empty, exactly like we talked about. 

But I don't want to... I don't want to stop living. I just want to feel *alive* again while I'm living, if you see what I mean. I want to actually *want* to paint my little watercolor trees again. My mother, God rest her soul, she always used to say that life is a gift, even when the wrapping paper is a bit torn and battered. She lived to be eighty-nine, right in the very same house I'm living in now, and she had her rough patches, certainly, but she always kept going. And I intend to keep going, too. I would never do anything to harm myself, I couldn't even fathom it. 

It's just that the days are so incredibly long right now. I just sit there in my chair and think, 'What on earth am I going to do with all this time?' But I never, ever think, 'I wish I didn't have the time.' It's more of a... a profound stuckness mixed with that heavy sludge feeling I mentioned earlier. So, no, to answer your question, no thoughts of hurting myself or checking out early. I just want the color to come back to things.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight over these past three months?

Well, food... food just doesn't hold the same appeal it used to, I suppose. It’s funny you ask that, because my wife—she's always been a wonderful cook, makes these lovely, hearty meals for us. Growing up, we were always taught you never, ever waste a scrap of food. 'Clean your plate,' my father used to say, and I always did! I was never one to leave anything behind, I always appreciated a good dinner. 

But lately, with this... this heavy feeling we’ve been discussing, I just don't even think about eating. I honestly have to consciously remind myself that it's time for a meal. If it weren't for the clock on the wall telling me it's noon or six o'clock, I might just sit there all day without taking a single bite. 

My wife has definitely noticed, too. She gets quite concerned, actually. Just the other evening, she made this wonderful chicken and wild rice soup—usually one of my absolute favorites, especially when the weather starts getting a bit chilly—and I just sat there pushing the spoon around. She pointed out that I was leaving my rice and soup half-finished. And that's happening almost every night now. Half a bowl of soup left, rice still sitting there getting cold in the bowl. 

And like I said, before all this started a few months ago, I would never waste a meal. Never. It's just... the desire simply isn't there anymore. Chewing almost feels like too much of a chore. So, yes, my appetite has certainly dropped off, and I imagine my weight might be slipping down a bit too, though I haven't actually stepped on the bathroom scale to check the exact numbers. It's just another thing that feels completely out of sorts right now.
Have you noticed changes in your energy level or how quickly you move and think—like feeling physically slowed down or restless—compared to before this started?

Well, slowed down... yes. That is exactly it. Restless, no, not at all, I don't have that nervous, pacing sort of energy. But slow? Heavens, yes. My entire body just feels incredibly slow, almost like I'm trying to move through a swimming pool full of molasses. 

Just the other morning, my wife asked if I could pop down to the corner store to pick up a carton of milk for her tea. It’s really not far at all—maybe three and a half blocks down the street, right past the old Methodist church with the red doors. I've made that walk a thousand times over the years, and normally I’d do it in ten, maybe twelve minutes tops. I always used to enjoy it, honestly, getting a little fresh air first thing. But lately... well, doing it now, it feels like I'm wearing boots made of solid lead. Every single step takes so much conscious effort, just having to tell my legs to lift up and move forward. By the time I finally got back to the house with that one little quart of milk, I had to sit down in the armchair for twenty minutes just to catch my breath, like I'd just hiked up a mountain. 

And it’s not even just the physical exertion of walking outside, either. It’s the smallest things right inside the house. Even just sitting at my desk... I have this lovely old oak roll-top desk in the corner of the living room where I handle our bills, and right now there’s a small mountain of retirement paperwork from the library that I need to go through. You would think, after thirty years of clerical work, I could sort a stack of papers in my sleep! I used to be so quick at it. But now, just lifting my arm to reach across the desk, or trying to sort a few envelopes into piles... it takes so much more effort than it ever should. My arms feel heavy, my hands feel clumsy, and I just sort of stare at the forms. It’s like the signal from my brain telling my hand to move is getting lost somewhere along the way. Everything just takes... well, it takes everything I have just to do the bare minimum.
Have you been feeling unusually worthless or guilty about things—perhaps blaming yourself for problems—more than you think is warranted?

Worthless? Guilty? Well... no, I wouldn't use those words. No, not at all. 

I know I said earlier that I feel a bit like a useless old piece of furniture sitting around the house, but I think that’s really just because I’m not *doing* anything right now. It's completely tied to my retirement from the library, you see. When you've spent three decades meticulously cataloging and sorting—and I mean meticulously, I had a color-coded system for the reference section that the head librarian herself commended at my little send-off party last month—well, you know your worth. You know you've done a good job. I've always been a hard worker. I never missed a day unless I was truly knocked flat, like that terrible flu that went around town back in '98. So, no, I certainly don't feel worthless as a person. I just feel like a person who currently doesn't have a task to do. 

And as for guilt... heavens, no. What on earth would I have to feel guilty about? My father, he was a very strict man, worked at the old manufacturing plant for forty-two years, and he always used to tell my brother and me that guilt is a heavy winter coat that only thieves and liars have to wear. And I've always tried to live a very honest, straightforward life. I've provided for my wife, I kept my section of the library running like an absolute Swiss watch, paid my taxes on time... 

I mean, I suppose if you want to split hairs, I feel a tiny bit bad that my wife is getting so terribly worried about me leaving my dinners half-finished, like with that lovely soup I was telling you about. You just hate to see your spouse fussing and fretting over you when they've gone to the trouble of cooking. But I don't sit in my chair blaming myself for this... this heavy sludge feeling. I didn't ask for it, after all! I didn't wake up one morning and decide to feel like I'm moving through a pool of molasses. It’s just something that seems to have settled over me. So, no, I don't sit around punishing myself or thinking I'm some sort of terrible burden or anything dramatic like that. I know I'm a good man. I just want to get back to being my usual self.

And my health... well, aside from this terrible gray fog and the heaviness we’ve been talking about, my physical health is quite alright. My regular doctor checked my cholesterol just last fall and told me I had the numbers of a man ten years younger. 

So, you see, there isn't really anything clear to worry about, and I don't find myself sitting around wringing my hands over the future out of nowhere. It’s actually quite the opposite of worry, if that makes any sense to you? Worry feels like... well, like your engine is revving too fast, like you’re pacing the floors and chewing your fingernails. I’m certainly not pacing. I can barely get myself out of the kitchen chair to even look at my watercolors, let alone pace. It’s more of a sinking feeling than a worrying one. I just sit there in the quiet, not really fretting over bills or what’s going to happen next year, just feeling completely stuck in the mud. So, no, no excessive worrying. Just... just that heavy, empty feeling.

inference.note: Patient denies excessive worry/anxiety symptoms, ruling out F41.1. Clear depressive symptoms present: depressed mood, anhedonia, cognitive fog/indecisiveness, duration >2 weeks (3 months), most days - consistent with major depressive episode.

doctor.intent: Assess sleep disturbance (initial insomnia, mid-night waking, or hypersomnia) as part of screening for major depressive episode criteria
doctor.question: How has your sleep been over these past three months—are you having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or sleeping more than usual?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: I go to bed tired, but I wake up around four in the morning and lie there thinking about what I am supposed to do with myself now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my sleep patterns, specifically if I have trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or sleeping more than usual, which matches the Sleep_Disturbance symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, sleep... sleep has become quite a trial lately, to be completely honest with you. It’s a strange thing, because you’d think with how heavy and exhausted I feel all day, I’d just sleep straight through till morning. And I do go to bed incredibly tired. By the time ten-thirty rolls around, after I've watched the local news—I never watch the national news right before bed, it's just too much noise—I am practically dragging myself down the hall to the bedroom. My bones just ache with that tiredness. 

So falling asleep isn't the issue at all. I usually drift off the minute my head hits the pillow. But staying asleep... well, that’s an entirely different story. 

Almost like clockwork, every single night, my eyes will just pop open. The room will be pitch black, and the house is so quiet you can hear the refrigerator humming all the way from the kitchen. I’ll roll over and look at the digital clock on my nightstand—it’s one of those older models with the bright red numbers, I think I bought it at a Sears back in the late nineties—and it almost always says four in the morning. Sometimes it's three-fifty-five, sometimes it's four-ten, but it is always right around four. 

And once I'm awake at that hour, that is simply the end of my sleep for the night. I don't toss and turn, really, I just lie there flat on my back, staring up at the ceiling in the dark. And my mind just gets stuck. I just lie there thinking about what I am supposed to do with myself now. You know, with leaving the library after thirty years, and having all this empty time stretching out ahead of me... I just stare into the dark, feeling that terrible heavy emptiness we talked about, and I wonder how I'm going to fill the hours if I can't even bring myself to pick up a paintbrush anymore. I don't feel panicked, exactly, it's not a racing feeling, but I just lie there for hours, wide awake, turning that same thought over and over until the sun finally comes up. It makes the days feel incredibly long, let me tell you.

inference.note: Early morning awakening, anhedonia, depressed mood, psychomotor slowing, and cognitive fog (concentration/indecisiveness) over 3 months, with GAD-type worry explicitly ruled out, continue to support a major depressive episode; no new findings suggest an alternative diagnosis.

doctor.intent: Assess for suicidal ideation or thoughts of self-harm, and feelings of worthlessness/guilt, given the depth of depressive symptoms already described
doctor.question: During this time, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, feeling like life isn't worth living, or that you'd be better off not being here?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal ideation or thoughts of death, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, heavens, no. No, no, nothing like that at all. I know I’ve been sitting here going on and on about this terrible gray fog, and how I just lie awake at four in the morning staring up at the ceiling, but... well, wanting to not be here? Hurting myself? No, absolutely not. 

It’s a very distinct difference, I think. I might feel like a useless old piece of furniture sitting in the kitchen, especially with my time at the library coming to a close. You know, when you’ve spent thirty years making sure the periodicals are perfectly organized—because let me tell you, some of the younger assistants, they just shove the magazines back on the shelves willy-nilly without checking the dates or the issue numbers—you get so used to having a clear, defined purpose. So losing that purpose makes me feel incredibly heavy and, well, empty, exactly like we talked about. 

But I don't want to... I don't want to stop living. I just want to feel *alive* again while I'm living, if you see what I mean. I want to actually *want* to paint my little watercolor trees again. My mother, God rest her soul, she always used to say that life is a gift, even when the wrapping paper is a bit torn and battered. She lived to be eighty-nine, right in the very same house I'm living in now, and she had her rough patches, certainly, but she always kept going. And I intend to keep going, too. I would never do anything to harm myself, I couldn't even fathom it. 

It's just that the days are so incredibly long right now. I just sit there in my chair and think, 'What on earth am I going to do with all this time?' But I never, ever think, 'I wish I didn't have the time.' It's more of a... a profound stuckness mixed with that heavy sludge feeling I mentioned earlier. So, no, to answer your question, no thoughts of hurting myself or checking out early. I just want the color to come back to things.

inference.note: Ruled out anxiety-related disorder (denies excessive worry) and no suicidal ideation, which supports MDD without psychotic features rather than alternative diagnoses. Core symptoms (depressed mood, anhedonia, early morning awakening, concentration/decision-making difficulty, duration >2 weeks tied to a stressor) remain consistent with a single depressive episode.

doctor.intent: Assess for changes in appetite or weight, another core criterion for major depressive disorder
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight over these past three months?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: I have to remind myself to eat, and my wife notices I leave rice and soup half-finished when before I would never waste a meal.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite or weight, which directly corresponds to the Weight_Appetite_Change symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Well, food... food just doesn't hold the same appeal it used to, I suppose. It’s funny you ask that, because my wife—she's always been a wonderful cook, makes these lovely, hearty meals for us. Growing up, we were always taught you never, ever waste a scrap of food. 'Clean your plate,' my father used to say, and I always did! I was never one to leave anything behind, I always appreciated a good dinner. 

But lately, with this... this heavy feeling we’ve been discussing, I just don't even think about eating. I honestly have to consciously remind myself that it's time for a meal. If it weren't for the clock on the wall telling me it's noon or six o'clock, I might just sit there all day without taking a single bite. 

My wife has definitely noticed, too. She gets quite concerned, actually. Just the other evening, she made this wonderful chicken and wild rice soup—usually one of my absolute favorites, especially when the weather starts getting a bit chilly—and I just sat there pushing the spoon around. She pointed out that I was leaving my rice and soup half-finished. And that's happening almost every night now. Half a bowl of soup left, rice still sitting there getting cold in the bowl. 

And like I said, before all this started a few months ago, I would never waste a meal. Never. It's just... the desire simply isn't there anymore. Chewing almost feels like too much of a chore. So, yes, my appetite has certainly dropped off, and I imagine my weight might be slipping down a bit too, though I haven't actually stepped on the bathroom scale to check the exact numbers. It's just another thing that feels completely out of sorts right now.

inference.note: Symptoms remain consistent with a single major depressive episode: depressed mood, anhedonia, cognitive fog/indecisiveness, early morning awakening, decreased appetite with likely weight loss, and situational trigger (retirement transition), without manic history, anxiety, or suicidal ideation to suggest alternative diagnoses.

doctor.intent: Assess presence of psychomotor retardation or agitation, and fatigue/energy loss
doctor.question: Have you noticed changes in your energy level or how quickly you move and think—like feeling physically slowed down or restless—compared to before this started?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: My body feels slow, like even walking to the corner store or sorting papers on my desk takes more effort than it should.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in physical movement, energy levels, or feeling slowed down/restless, which maps directly to psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Well, slowed down... yes. That is exactly it. Restless, no, not at all, I don't have that nervous, pacing sort of energy. But slow? Heavens, yes. My entire body just feels incredibly slow, almost like I'm trying to move through a swimming pool full of molasses. 

Just the other morning, my wife asked if I could pop down to the corner store to pick up a carton of milk for her tea. It’s really not far at all—maybe three and a half blocks down the street, right past the old Methodist church with the red doors. I've made that walk a thousand times over the years, and normally I’d do it in ten, maybe twelve minutes tops. I always used to enjoy it, honestly, getting a little fresh air first thing. But lately... well, doing it now, it feels like I'm wearing boots made of solid lead. Every single step takes so much conscious effort, just having to tell my legs to lift up and move forward. By the time I finally got back to the house with that one little quart of milk, I had to sit down in the armchair for twenty minutes just to catch my breath, like I'd just hiked up a mountain. 

And it’s not even just the physical exertion of walking outside, either. It’s the smallest things right inside the house. Even just sitting at my desk... I have this lovely old oak roll-top desk in the corner of the living room where I handle our bills, and right now there’s a small mountain of retirement paperwork from the library that I need to go through. You would think, after thirty years of clerical work, I could sort a stack of papers in my sleep! I used to be so quick at it. But now, just lifting my arm to reach across the desk, or trying to sort a few envelopes into piles... it takes so much more effort than it ever should. My arms feel heavy, my hands feel clumsy, and I just sort of stare at the forms. It’s like the signal from my brain telling my hand to move is getting lost somewhere along the way. Everything just takes... well, it takes everything I have just to do the bare minimum.

inference.note: Psychomotor retardation, anhedonia, early morning awakening, decreased appetite, and slowed cognition/movement further support major depressive episode with melancholic features. No manic/hypomanic history reported, no excessive worry pattern suggesting GAD, and no anxiety-driven symptoms. Candidate list remains unchanged, though features are consistent with melancholic subtype of MDD.

doctor.intent: Assess for feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, a core depressive symptom not yet explored
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually worthless or guilty about things—perhaps blaming yourself for problems—more than you think is warranted?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worthless? Guilty? Well... no, I wouldn't use those words. No, not at all. 

I know I said earlier that I feel a bit like a useless old piece of furniture sitting around the house, but I think that’s really just because I’m not *doing* anything right now. It's completely tied to my retirement from the library, you see. When you've spent three decades meticulously cataloging and sorting—and I mean meticulously, I had a color-coded system for the reference section that the head librarian herself commended at my little send-off party last month—well, you know your worth. You know you've done a good job. I've always been a hard worker. I never missed a day unless I was truly knocked flat, like that terrible flu that went around town back in '98. So, no, I certainly don't feel worthless as a person. I just feel like a person who currently doesn't have a task to do. 

And as for guilt... heavens, no. What on earth would I have to feel guilty about? My father, he was a very strict man, worked at the old manufacturing plant for forty-two years, and he always used to tell my brother and me that guilt is a heavy winter coat that only thieves and liars have to wear. And I've always tried to live a very honest, straightforward life. I've provided for my wife, I kept my section of the library running like an absolute Swiss watch, paid my taxes on time... 

I mean, I suppose if you want to split hairs, I feel a tiny bit bad that my wife is getting so terribly worried about me leaving my dinners half-finished, like with that lovely soup I was telling you about. You just hate to see your spouse fussing and fretting over you when they've gone to the trouble of cooking. But I don't sit in my chair blaming myself for this... this heavy sludge feeling. I didn't ask for it, after all! I didn't wake up one morning and decide to feel like I'm moving through a pool of molasses. It’s just something that seems to have settled over me. So, no, I don't sit around punishing myself or thinking I'm some sort of terrible burden or anything dramatic like that. I know I'm a good man. I just want to get back to being my usual self.

inference.note: Patient endorses depressed mood, anhedonia, cognitive fog/concentration difficulty, early morning awakening insomnia, appetite/weight loss, and psychomotor retardation over 3 months, meeting criteria for a major depressive episode. No excessive worry (rules out GAD), no worthlessness/guilt, no suicidal ideation. Symptom profile remains consistent with a single major depressive episode without psychotic features.
